title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 256
paragraphs: The clean males of the ox kind, then, both full-grown animals and calves, are sacrificed by all the Egyptians; but the females they may not sacrifice, for these are sacred to Isis. The figure of Isis is in the form of a woman with cow's horns, just as the Hellenes represent Io in pictures, and all the Egyptians without exception revere cows far more than any other kind of cattle. For this reason no Egyptian man or woman would kiss a Hellene on the mouth, nor will they use a knife, roasting-spits, or cauldron belonging to a Hellene, nor taste of the flesh even of a clean animal if it has been cut with a Hellene's knife. They bury the cattle of this kind that die in the following manner. The females they throw into the river, but the males they bury, each people in the outskirts of their town, with one of the horns (or sometimes both) protruding to mark the place. When the bodies have rotted away and the appointed time comes, then to each city comes a boat from what is called the island of Prosopitis (this is in the Delta, and the circuit of it measures nine schoeni). On this island of Prosopitis, besides many other cities, stands the one from which the boats come to collect the bones of the oxen; the city's name is Atarbechis, and in it there is a holy temple of Aphrodite. From this city many go out in various directions, some to one city and some to another, and when they have dug up the bones of the oxen they carry them off, and all together they bury them in a single place. In the same way they bury their other cattle when these die, for the same law is laid down concerning them, and these too they abstain from killing.
